1.goal: To hear one opinion from her about something she chose, before any model reaches the screen — this is the baseline the whole cycle is measured against — and to tell her what the lesson ends with.
1.interaction: T–S, spoken. She answers out loud; nothing is written down here.
run: Ask whether she opened the pre-class and whether anything in it was unclear.
Tell her what the lesson ends with: two reviews to read, and then a recommendation of her own, out loud, with two reasons. One sentence is enough.
Ask the question on screen. Take the title and the yes or no, and move on: the reasons are the work of the rest of the hour, not of this screen.
exact: About the pre-class: “Did you open the pre-class? Was anything hard?”
What today is: “Today you read two reviews. Then you recommend something you watched — with two reasons.”
If she names something and stops: “Would you tell a friend to watch it?”
1.expected: Two pieces of information and no more: a title, and yes or no to “would you tell a friend to watch it?” A complete answer at this point looks like “Wednesday, season two. Yes.” — the title and the verdict, with no reason attached. If a reason does arrive without you asking for it, write down her exact words: that is the habit the cycle exists to build, and this is the screen where you measure it before the lesson has taught anything.
1.support: If nothing comes to mind, name two categories out loud and let her pick one: the last thing she watched to the end, or the last thing she stopped watching. Choosing between two is easier than producing from nothing, and what she does next is the same.
1.challenge: Ask who she would recommend it to, and who she would not. It is the first push toward a reason without naming it as one.
1.monitoring: Whether a reason appears without being asked for. This is the baseline of the whole block.
1.evidence: Whether a reason came unprompted, and how many sentences she produced in one turn.
1.transition: Move on as soon as she has named something and heard what the lesson ends with.

2.goal: To have her hear, before she has to produce anything, the difference between an answer that gives the other person something to say back and one that leaves them with nothing.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the five answers on screen together.
run: Read the situation on screen with her.
Read the five answers out loud, one at a time, and ask which ones give the other person something to answer.
Do not judge them one by one as you read. Take all five, then close the screen with the two that carry a reason.
exact: Setting the task: “Someone asks you if the movie is good. Which of these answers gives them something to say back?”
Closing the screen: “Two of them say what you think and then why. The other three leave the other person with nothing to answer — that is where the conversation stops.”
2.expected: The two that work are “It is good, because the characters feel real.” and “It is slow, but that is why I liked it.” Both carry a reason. The three that do not are “It is good.”, “Yeah.” and “I do not know.” — a verdict, or not even that, with nothing for the other person to pick up.
2.support: If she picks the short ones, read “Yeah.” again and ask what the other person could possibly say next.
2.challenge: Ask which of the two working answers she is more likely to say herself, and why.
2.monitoring: Whether she can hear the difference before she can produce it.
2.evidence: Whether she named the reason as the part that does the work, and in what words.
2.transition: Move on once the two useful answers have been named.

3.goal: To have her commit to a guess about why two people disagree about the same movie, before she reads a word of either review, so that the reading has something to confirm or refute.
3.interaction: T–S, guessing out loud. Nothing is confirmed or corrected here.
run: Read the three questions on screen with her.
Take one guess on each. Do not confirm and do not correct: these are hypotheses, and the reading is what settles them.
Write her guesses on the first two questions somewhere she can see them. She checks them herself on the next screen.
exact: If she risks nothing: “Guess: is it about the story, or about the people?”
Before moving on: “That is your guess. Now we read and see if you were right.”
3.expected: There is no answer key on this screen: the three questions are open, and nothing is right or wrong yet. What the reviews will show, two screens from now: Maya's reason is the people (“the two main characters feel like real people”), Chris's is the story (“a story you can guess in ten minutes”), and yes, both are right about the same movie. Do not say any of it here.
3.support: If she risks nothing, name two possibilities and let her choose one. Choosing is still risking.
3.challenge: Ask whether a bad review can be useful to someone who ends up liking the movie.
3.monitoring: Whether she guesses without being sure. She tolerates being wrong well, so this should come easily.
3.evidence: Her two predictions, written down for the next screen.
3.transition: Move on when all three have an answer, right or wrong.

4.goal: To read both reviews once and come out knowing which one recommends the movie and which one does not: the position of each, before any detail.
run: Give her about a minute and a half for the two of them together.
Ask which one recommends the movie and which one does not.
Ask which of her guesses from the screen before turned out to be right.
exact: Before she reads: “Read both once. You only need one thing: which one says watch it.”
4.expected: Maya recommends it: her review ends on “Worth watching.” Chris does not: his ends on “I would not recommend it.” Both verdicts are in the last sentence of each review, and that is the whole answer this screen asks for. On the guesses from the screen before: Maya's reason is the people, Chris's is the story, and the third question is a yes.
4.support: If a word stops her, tell her to leave it and carry on; if it still matters at the end, come back to it then.
4.challenge: Ask which of the two reviews she would have written, before she looks at the reasons.
4.monitoring: Whether she reads for the whole first, or tries to decode line by line. Nothing in the previous seventeen lessons asked her to read on her own, so this is the first thing you will know about it.
4.evidence: How long she takes, and whether she has to reread to answer.
4.transition: Move on once she has named who says watch it.

5.goal: To attribute each of the six reasons to the reviewer who gave it, and to go back to the text to show the line that proves it.
5.interaction: S alone on the activity, then T–S to check.
run: Let her place all six on her own, and press Check when she has finished. The button checks the whole exercise at once, so let her get to the end before anything is marked.
Then go through the six out loud, in order, and on each one ask her to point at the line in the review that proves it.
Spend what is left on the last one, the photography. It is the one that teaches something.
exact: On the photography item: “Chris did not like the movie. So why is this sentence in his review?”
5.expected: Three each. Maya: “The two main characters feel like real people.” · “The ending stays with you for days.” · “It is slow, and that is the point.” Chris: “You can guess the story in ten minutes.” · “Two hours is a long time for this story.” · “The photography is beautiful.” The first five come out easily. The sixth is the one that surprises, because it is praise sitting inside the negative review.
5.support: If she is stuck on one, narrow it to a choice: who talks about time, the one who liked it or the one who did not?
5.challenge: Ask her to find the one thing both reviews mention. It is the ending.
5.monitoring: Whether she goes back to the text to sustain an answer, or answers from memory.
5.evidence: Whether she returned to the text when asked to prove something, and on which items.
5.transition: Move on when the six are placed and the photography one has been discussed.

6.goal: To separate what the reviews actually say from what she assumes they say.
6.interaction: S alone, then T–S to check, with the reviews behind the button on screen.
run: Let her mark the three she thinks are true and press Check.
Go through the six out loud. On each true one, ask which line says it, and open Show the reviews if she cannot remember.
The theater item is the one that is nowhere in the text. Make that explicit when you reach it.
6.expected: True: “Both reviews talk about the ending.” (Maya: it stays with you; Chris: it is the only surprise and it comes too late.) · “Chris finds something good in the movie.” (“The photography is beautiful.”) · “Chris thinks the story is easy to guess.” (“a story you can guess in ten minutes”). False: “Maya thinks the movie is too slow.” — she says it is slow and that this is the point, so slow is her reason to watch it. · “Maya recommends the movie because of the photography.” — she never mentions the photography; that is Chris. · “Both reviewers saw the movie at a theater.” — neither of them says where they saw it, and this one is not in the text at all.
6.support: If she marks the theater one, open the reviews and ask her to find the word theater in either of them.
6.challenge: Ask what the two reviews would have to say for them to be about different movies.
6.monitoring: Whether she tells what is written from what sounds likely. It comes back in the fourth block.
6.evidence: Which of the three false ones she marked, if any.
6.transition: Move on once the six are settled.

7.goal: To have her notice that the lines of a review do three different jobs, before anyone names the three.
run: Let her sort the six lines on her own and press Check.
Go through them, and on each reason ask what the other person can do with it.
Do not name the rule here. The next screen is where it lands.
7.expected: Two of each. An opinion: “It is slow, and that is the point.” · “I do not agree.” A reason: “The two main characters feel like real people.” · “Two hours is a long time for a story you can guess in ten minutes.” A recommendation: “Worth watching.” · “I would not recommend it.” The long Chris line is the one most often called an opinion: it sounds like a complaint, and it is the reason underneath the complaint.
7.support: Ask, on each line: could someone argue with this? An opinion cannot be argued with; a reason can be used.
7.challenge: Ask which of the three jobs is missing from most of what people say when they are asked about a movie.
7.monitoring: Whether she sees the function of a line and not only its content.
7.evidence: Whether she identified the reason as the usable part without being told.
7.transition: Move on when the six are sorted and she has said, in her own words, what a reason does.

8.goal: To show her, with the reasons taken away, that an opinion on its own does not let anyone decide anything, and that adding the reason is what makes the same sentence usable.
8.interaction: T–S, with the three reveal buttons on screen.
run: Read the two lines on screen: this is what is left of each review when the reason is removed.
Ask the question on screen: with only these two lines, would she watch the movie?
Open the first two buttons and read the two complete sentences out loud. The difference should be audible.
Open the third button last and read the three jobs with her. This is the point of the lesson, and it lands here.
8.expected: She cannot decide from the two short lines: one says it is worth watching, the other says he would not recommend it, and there is nothing to weigh. Behind the first two buttons, the same two sentences with the reason attached: “It is worth watching, because the two main characters feel like real people.” and “I would not recommend it, because you can guess the whole story in ten minutes.” Now she can decide, and the only thing that changed is the reason. Behind the third: the opinion is what you think and nobody can argue with it, the reason is the part the other person can use, the recommendation is what they asked for.
8.support: If she says she would decide anyway, ask what she would be deciding on.
8.challenge: Ask which of the two complete sentences she finds more convincing, and why.
8.monitoring: Whether the point lands as something she noticed rather than something she was told.
8.evidence: Her own words for why the reason matters. Write them down if they are good.
8.transition: Move on to production once the three buttons have been read.

9.goal: To produce one whole sentence — opinion and reason together — about four titles she names herself.
9.interaction: T–S, spoken, one title at a time.
run: Collect the four titles first. Read the four boxes on screen and ask her to name one real title for each. Write the four down where you can see them: the repertoire is hers, and this is the only part of the screen that has to be built before it can be run.
Then name one of her four back to her. She answers in one sentence: what she thinks, and why.
Take all four, one after the other, without stopping to correct.
Praise the whole sentence, not the correct word. The sentence is what the block is measuring.
exact: Collecting the titles: “Give me a real name for each of these four. Anything you have actually watched or read.”
If she answers with an opinion only: “Good. Now say it again with the reason in the same sentence.”
9.expected: Four sentences, each with a reason inside it. The titles are hers, so there is no key here: what is being checked is the shape, and the shape is on screen — “I think it is worth watching, because…” or “I would not recommend it, because…”. Four out of four is the target; three is already more than she has been doing.
9.support: If she stops after the opinion, give the first two words of the reason and let her finish it.
9.challenge: Ask for one of the four without her reading the sentence starters.
9.monitoring: Whether the reason comes in the same breath or as a second turn after a prompt.
9.evidence: How many of the four carried a reason unprompted, and the four titles she named. They are the repertoire for the rest of the block.
9.transition: Move on when all four have been said.

10.goal: To say two reasons in the same turn, and to tell a genuinely second reason apart from the first one said again in other words.
run: Ask her to take one of the four titles from the screen before and say it again, this time with two reasons in the same turn.
Use the box on screen to check that the second reason is a second one, and not the first repeated.
Do it twice, with two different titles.
exact: If the second reason repeats the first: “That is the same reason in other words. Give me a different one — about the ending, or the people, or how long it is.”
10.expected: Two reasons in one turn, from two different places. The box on screen carries the model: “It is boring, and nothing happens” is one reason said twice, because both halves are about the same thing; “It is slow, and the ending does not pay off” is two, because one is about the pace and the other about the ending. Two titles done this way is what this screen asks for.
10.support: Name three places a second reason can come from — the people, the story, or how long it is — and let her pick one.
10.challenge: Ask for a third reason, or for the reason she thinks someone else would give.
10.monitoring: Whether she can tell two reasons apart from one reason said twice.
10.evidence: Whether a second, distinct reason appeared, and whether it needed prompting.
10.transition: Move on when she has produced two distinct reasons at least once.

11.goal: To speak for longer than one turn about something she chose, to someone who has never heard of it: what it is, what she thinks, two reasons, and what the listener should do — with the sentence starters closed.
11.interaction: T–S, sustained. She talks; you listen and do not correct.
run: Give her one minute to decide what she will talk about and, if she wants, to write two words down. She likes preparation time, and one minute is enough here.
Ask her to tell you about it as if you had never heard of it. Do not interrupt for language.
Point her to the button with the sentence starters only if she stalls.
exact: Opening the task: “I have never heard of this. Tell me what it is, what you think, and why — and tell me what I should do about it.”
If she stops after two sentences: “And what else? Give me the other reason.”
11.expected: Four things in one turn: what it is, what she thinks, two different reasons, and a recommendation. The four items on screen are the checklist — tick them as they arrive and note which one is missing. Three to five sentences. Two or three is where she has been until now, so anything past that is the result of the hour.
11.support: The starters are behind a closed button. Open them only if she stalls, let her look, and close them again: with them on screen she reads instead of speaking.
11.challenge: Ask her to convince you after you have said that you do not usually like that kind of thing.
11.monitoring: Count the sentences and count the distinct reasons. Note whether she asked how to say a word, and which word.
11.evidence: How many sentences in one turn, how many distinct reasons, and whether the button stayed closed. This is the main record of the lesson.
11.transition: Move on when she has finished her turn.

12.goal: To keep her talking once the prepared turn is over: to answer a real question about the thing she recommended, add something nobody asked for, and put a question back to you.
12.interaction: T–S, unscripted. This is a conversation, not a task.
run: Ask two questions about the thing itself, not about English: what happens in it, who else would like it, why she started watching it. Ask what you actually want to know.
After each answer, wait. The silence is where the extra sentence comes from, and filling it is what stops her.
Then ask her to put one question back to you about it. Answer it, and let the exchange run one more turn if it wants to.
exact: Opening: “I want to know more about it. Who is in it, and what happens?”
If she answers in one clause and stops: “And what else? Tell me one more thing about it.”
Handing the turn over: “Now ask me something about it.”
12.expected: Two answers that go past what the question asked for, and one question from her. A whole answer here looks like “It is about a girl who moves to a new school, and the best part is when she finds out her friend lied to her” — the answer, and then something nobody asked for. Her question back can be as small as “Have you watched it?”: what is being checked is that it exists at all, because it is what turns an answer into a conversation.
12.support: If she answers and stops, do not ask the same question again in other words. Name one thing you would like to know — the ending, the people, how long it is — and let her choose which to talk about.
12.challenge: Disagree with her about one thing and let her defend it. It is a preview of the next screen.
12.monitoring: Whether her answers run longer than the question asked for, and whether the question back comes without you asking for it.
12.evidence: How many turns the exchange lasted, and whether she asked a question of her own.
12.transition: Move on when she has answered two questions and asked one.

13.goal: To give her one piece of feedback she can act on, and then run the same recommendation in a different situation: this time the listener has already seen it and disagrees.
run: Name one thing that worked and one thing to build on, and write both in the boxes on screen.
Put her first version and a clearer version of the same sentence side by side in the two boxes below.
Open the replay. This time you have already seen it and did not like it: she keeps her two reasons and adds one thing she agrees with you about.
exact: Opening the replay: “I have seen it, and it did not work for me. Tell me why it worked for you.”
13.expected: The same two reasons she gave two screens ago, plus one concession, in the shape of the line on screen: “You are right about…, but…” A complete second version sounds like “You are right about the beginning, it is slow, but the two of them feel like real people and the ending stays with you.” The concession is the new part and will need the line on screen the first time. What is being checked is that the two reasons survive the disagreement instead of shrinking to one.
13.support: Point at the line on screen and let her use it word for word on the first attempt.
13.challenge: If the concession is not really a concession, ask what she actually agrees with.
13.monitoring: Whether the reasons hold up under disagreement, or reduce to one.
13.evidence: Whether she conceded a point and still held her position. It is the first sign of the third block.
13.transition: Move on when the second version has been said.

14.goal: To close on what was worked on, to let her say how confident she feels about it, and to leave the homework said out loud.
14.interaction: T–S, going through the recap and the confidence scale together.
run: Go through the recap list with her and tick what was done.
Let her fill the confidence scale herself.
Read the three lines on the right and say the homework out loud.
exact: The homework, said out loud: “Next time you finish an episode, before you close it, decide what you would say about it — and the reason.”
14.expected: The recap has six lines, and all six were done if the lesson ran to the end: reading the two reviews, telling the opinion from the reason, finding the line that supports an answer, saying what she thinks and why in one turn, giving two different reasons, and recommending something of her own without the screen. The confidence scale is hers, and it may come out lower than what you saw.
14.support: If she marks everything low, name one specific thing she did today that she could not do an hour ago.
14.challenge: Ask which of today's phrases she would use in Portuguese too.
14.monitoring: Whether her self-assessment matches what you observed. The gap is worth noting.
14.evidence: Her confidence marks, and anything she said about the pre-class.
14.transition: End here. The next lesson opens with the same two people, talking.
